segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh, there was a story about Lou and Perry from Colorado. There was a story about Lou and Perry from Colorado, about a cat in a stove. Would you tell me that story?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, you know, that snow has been pretty deep and the cold, you know, and finally I got so that they could get outside their shutdown for three days in the bed because the water was so deep in the house that they couldn't get out. And they left a cat in and then she jumped off and over on the oven door and went into the leg down in the oven. Well, when they come in, they shut the oven door and never thought about it and built up a fire and then they roasted the cat in. So they burnt the feet off from her and they had to kill the cat.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How did they find out the cat was in there?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Because it got a stick in the bad cabin and they would go to look all over and see what was burning up and it was the cat that they roasted the hair off from.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How come it was flooding? Did it flood here much? Huh? Did it flood much in those days?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Hell, in our house, the house stood down there on the flat. By God, the water come in the house so it went right up again the mattress in the bed. Hell, I've seen that flat in there after it was cleared up, a regular skating rink. Hell, you could skate all over that mattress.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How long would it flood for?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh, several days.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What month? What month would be the high month?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, it would generally be along in March when the snow started going bad and it started raining and snow up here six feet deep and the mud got full of water and started breaking through. By God, there would be water all over.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How high above the creek was your place?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, it was just put right down the level of the bank. It was there for three years and then moved up on the hillside here.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Why did you move it? Huh? Why did your father move it?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Because it was too wet down there. All the neighbors got together and tore the house down and moved it and set it up again in one day.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Everybody just pitched in help like that?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: You're damn right. And by God, there were neighbors two days. It ain't like it is now. And by God, put in here every Saturday night they'd all get together and they'd have a good time. And when they'd meet on the road, they'd always stop and talk. Now, when you meet your neighbor, they just drive faster and look the other way. Neighbors are called anymore.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you exchange work a lot with your neighbors?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yes, quite a little.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did you do?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: I did that because I was too young to begin with. But, well, I've had this place since 1911. So I've been here quite a while too… and of course,… the folks moved on the first 1891.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: These winners, were there heavy snow winners that you remember?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yes. Hell, there was nothing to see six and seven feet of snow here. By God, Bovill had nine. Elk River had 13 feet of snow.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How did you get by when the snow was so deep?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, mostly stay home and if you wanted to go on your horse, it was mostly skis or web shoes. Well, all the... all got a few sheaves and they cut the wool off from them and spin and make join. And the women, they'd never go to a neighbor unless there'd be a knitting socks or something. When they knit, there was five needles in the knitting needles for... To knit on, there was one extra that they thread the loops on and over on the main needle. And the Americans, they generally used a crochet hook and crocheted sweaters for the kids. Now, I've seen good many hard times and I hope some of these kids now, they'll never see anything like it. But I've lived through it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you remember the cabin that Joe Wells had?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yeah, it was just a little old cabin. With the ..., it was... I'm now excited with the little awful little I'm being said. The Indian kids, I wasn't a bit afraid of them, but the nigger kids, they were too damn polite. I was a little spooky of them, but they got damn good friends of mine.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did Roy and Chuck used to play pranks a lot?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Roy, yeah, Chuck, he used to play the harp, mouth harp. And boy, he liked to dance too… and that was from an egg. Well,… the white girls around here, they wasn't a better master. They'd dance with them nigger boys just as well as anybody else. And boy, we'd just as soon dance with them nigger girls as any other.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What kind of music did he play with his mouth harp?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yeah, it was waltzes and quadrilles and stuff like that. He played at the dances. Oh yeah, and then the loins just come in and they all... there was four boys and they all played the fiddle a little and the girls had played the banjo and the guitar. Oh heck, I'll tell you, it was lots of fun too, and by god, they were all nervous.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would you dance in the schoolhouse? Is that where you'd dance?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh yeah, there were a good many dancers in the old nigger schoolhouse. And old Joe Wells, he couldn't dance, but boy, he'd get up and dance a jig. Especially when they're starting playing old black Joe.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh, is that true? Was Joe a pretty strong man?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh yeah, he was a pretty husky nigger.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Why do they call that his schoolhouse?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Wells was built on his place, on the corner of his place, so they called it the Wells Schoolhouse.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Who built it, do you know?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, all the neighbors got together and cut the logs and built it and Joe had a single horse and they used that one horse to roll the logs up.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So he gave him the land? He gave him the land?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yeah, he gave him the chance to bed on the land. And when they got to their schoolhouse, then Joe's daughter lived in the old schoolhouse for years. And there's one thing I'm mad about, that then god damn bastards had to tear that schoolhouse down and burn it up. They should have left it. So people could have seen what went on in olden days.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: That's where you went to school, right?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yes.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you spend much time with Joe, around Joe?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh yeah, you know, he had three kids, was together with the kids. They had one dog up there that got to rabies and they didn't have to get out. And I was over at Andrew's, I was pretty well grown up and nigga Mary come over there and the dog had the rabies, she sneaked out through the back door. And they had a gun down there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well I went down, I killed the dog, all right? Was she a good cook?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: None better… she had been a cook for the Welsh boys while she was a young girl. While she was a slave girl. By god no, she could cook just as good as any woman in the country. She'd been a slave back in Carolina, just like Joe… she took that… well she was Joe's wife. So when the Welsh boys come out they brought him. And the Welsh boys, you know on this side of Moscow there is a deep cut there and there is some buildings right across the cut there. There is where the Welsh boys died.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well did the Welsh boys treat Joe like a brother?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: You're damn right they did. And they even helped Joe build the cabin up here. Then Joe's kids, hell they were down at the Welsh boys half of the time. And Frank Welsh was a good blacksmith. He done the blacksmithing all the people up in here and come was a good cook. And boy you never could come down there if it was around meal time unless you had to come in and have dinner with him. Frank had little black mustache and come was always smooth shaved. But he was lighter color.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you ever hear that Old Man Wells back in Carolina had given Joe money just like he gave Frank and Crom money to come out here?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: No, but they took Joe right along with him. So they all come in the same bunch.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did many people stop and eat at the Wells place?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: By God, everybody went up and down the road stopping at them. Even Bovill had a good many meals at Joe Wells.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would there be a lot of people there for a meal? Do you think there would be more than a couple of people there for a meal? Would a whole bunch of people eat there?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh hell, sometimes they'd have a house full. And Joe, you know, he liked to drink. Well they'd stop and feed their horses. And he'd always have a bottle down in the barn and give them teamsters a drink. And boy, they always was willing to stop there. And hell, whiskey, you know, they would buy it for $3 a gallon those days. And now, my God, $5, $6 for a fifth.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you ever hear of Joe getting into trouble with Marshall Hayes and Troy?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh, he got in trouble every once in a while.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: But you know, with Hayes you mean?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yeah. Yes, and by God, Andrew Olson was there and he took Joe Wells' part. And by God, Hayes went out through the door head first. And then Joe happened to be married to my older sister. I heard Joe used to go to Troy with some of the other boys from around here and they'd have a good time. The damn right they'd have a good time. Joe wasn't a damn bit stingy neither. By God, he'd treat just as fast as any of them. And Chuck was the same way. But Troy, he wasn't much to drink. He kept pretty sober all the time.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How did Joe make a living?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh, hell, as quick as the starting loggin'. Hell, he had some of the best horses in the country and he logged. By God, now he took in some real logs. Oh, boy, they were good loggers and by God, he had a couple Irishmen that was working for him and by God, they wouldn't work for nobody else but Joe Wells.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Are you saying that Joe was a real hard worker?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: The damn right old Joe would work. Chuck wasn't a... he'd work but you know he had diabetical ... So he had to be by his one leg and he had to keep that pack was cuttin' all the time.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Where did Joe log? Did he have an operation for logging?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, you know, anybody that had logs to sell to the company, he'd take the job and haul the log in. And he'd get so much to sell and put logs in him and the owners that owned the log would get so much. No, old Joe was alright. I've heard that Lou used to have sheep. Oh, yeah. Yes, they had sheep and she had a great big high -spinning wheel. I think it must have been damn close to seven feet tall. And she'd turn nuts with her hand and spin yarn and then she'd knit German socks for the men.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: German socks? What's that?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, they were big high socks that would go clean up to the knee. Had a joint in German socks or felt boots, neither one.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What boots? What kind of boots?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Felt boots. They were heavy -filled and by God they were about name -shake. And that leached right up to the knee. I've seen them and I wore them too. Hmm. So, you're telling me about Joe that nobody cared whether he was black or not. Nobody cared. Everybody liked him anyway… damn right… no one from the built to Lutheran church, by God, old Joe, put in his church or built that too. Well, the first Christmas, they had a Christmas tree down there. And the nigger kids all over the side, Joe, and they all got a bag of candy. And boy, them nigger kids were tickled. I guess maybe they never had a bag of candy. No, when a fellow sits and thinks back, that pudding of air makes the fellow cry.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did your father have something to do with the first church being built?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, he is the one that got the plot for the church and he bagged quite a lot of money for it. And by God, the fellow that had the place that the church was built on, he gave them the timber. And they logged the timber down to the mill and Pete Dahlbergs sold it out for lumber. And if they furnished a man, he furnished a mill to sell out to lumber. Well, they got short of money and I and this old Martin Olson, we split the shingles for the north side of the church. Martin split them and I shaved them for the north side of the church. And it was all volunteer work. And now, it's all been volunteer work. Well, there's a bunch of Californians come in. By God, they even tried to show us how to walk on the road.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You don't think they're doing much for the country, huh?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: No, you're damn right. This neighbor over here, he tried to fence in the road too. And just leave a little street here, ten feet wide. But by God, I've seen too that the sheriff come out and had a pretty good long talk with him. So he had to move back his fences.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you remember Nils Lund, the miner? Do you remember that foolish miner name of Nils Lund?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: He's over on Boulder Creek. Yeah, you bet I remember. Nils and his brother Martin.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was he like?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh, they were pretty heavy fellows. They were Swedes. I thought Nils was sort of a crazy guy. Yeah, that one of them was. Nils was kind of crazy. He went to go back to Sweden and he died at sea. And I guess he was buried right in the ocean. Because it took seventeen days to cross the ocean.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Why was Nils, what was it about Nils that was funny? What was it about this fellow that he was sort of a funny guy?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yeah, he wasn't all that. He always says there's bad news North America.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: He meant this crazy North America, this country here. No, he didn't like it here at all. He was going back to Sweden.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: He said this country was crazy?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did he ever tell you why?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: No. But he'd get out and work every summer so he always had a little money so he could get along. He had a homestead over there. But then the monkeys with him, you know, over in Moscow and tried to put him in the asylum and he never would want to go back to Moscow and prove up. So he sold the homestead for fifty dollars and then he was going back to Sweden. You know, some of these people, the worst damn thing they can do is to monkey with half crazy people. Because if you leave them alone, you can get along pretty good with them. But if you monkey with them, you'll just make them that much worse.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was it about him that made people think he wasn't all there? What did he do that made people think he was half crazy?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, you know, he wouldn't socialize with anybody about the only damn place. It'd be he'd stop here once in a while. Because Dad was one of these fellows, you know, he could get along with anybody. If they wanted to say something, my God, Dad would help them along.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: If they wanted to say something?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yeah, if they were talking, I got Dad to help them ride along. And Dad would have a melapin after a little bit. Your dad, he just liked people. Oh yeah, Dad could get along with anybody. And Mother was the same way. There's a story I heard about this Lund, this man. The story was that he used to mine. He said he would mine where a tree pointed. He thought God was showing him where he should dig his holes in the ground. Oh yeah. Yes, he believed in God alright. And that's a whole lot more than a lot of them do. And if you stop and think about it, there is some great power that handles this world too. It isn't a people.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Arthur, why do you think that? Why do you say that? Why isn't it the people?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, the people think they know it all. But you take and go out and you do something wrong.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, you get kind of scared, don't you?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Just so nobody don't catch you.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: By gosh, it's your heart that told you that you have done something wrong and it kind of scares you a little, don't it?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: No, by George, I fully believe there is some great overpower from somewhere. But there is a lot of people that don't think that. Oh, I was going to ask you if you remember Big Anderson.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you remember him?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: He was an old hermit that lived...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Who?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: His name was Big Anderson. He lived by Anderson Crossing and he was sort of a hermit.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Remember him?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yeah, we called him Big Anderson.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was he like?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: He was a pretty heavy sort of a man. And God, he called him the wild animal. That is the devil. That was the wild animal and the man above.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: That was God?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: That was supposed to be God.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did he talk about religion?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh, not too much, a little. But you know, he had one of the nice response on Barrett. And then he laid down there by the creek and prospected and dug holes in the hills to find gold and rented the place. That is something, you know, them prospectors, by gosh, if they seem like they have to be digging in the ground all the time, it does not make any difference how good the place they got. They leave that layer alone and rent it to somebody else. It is just a kind of a damn fever. He did not do very good at prospecting. No. Like them old prospectors, there was none of them that done anything. Now there was an old fella up here. His name was Pete Jackson. He laid up there and prospected for years and he had two of the best farms in the Genesee country and had them rented away. And he spent all the money he got down there up there in the prospect hole.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Where did he prospect?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Up on Ruby Creek. I thought lots of times if my eyes were so I could see, I would like to go up there and see what that old prospect looked like today where he was.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you see it in the old days?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: That is the damn right I did. And it is right where they call it the Jackson Butte right now.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What? How did he do? He did not do very good either?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Hell, I do not think he ever made a dollar out of that prospect. I think he spent every dollar he got up from the farm. Sometimes he had a little fella by the name of Joe Emang to come up there and help him. And that Joe Emang, he went back to the old country.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you know, was he just using a placer? Just placer mining or was he doing more than that?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh, hell, Christ, there was tunnels that were 100 feet long. There is one tunnel right over across the creek here that was put in over 80 years ago. That tunnel is 127 feet long and I have been to the bottom of a circle. Dyers usually go in there and hibernate during the winter.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you know who dug the tunnel here? Do you know who dug this tunnel here?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: His name was Day. There were three, four of them days. There was a Day day, an Irish day, and a Mark day.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: They live around here? Were they here in this country?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yeah, one of them had a farm right down here… and, now, Irish Day, he had a cabin out there. And it wouldn't surprise me unless cabin still stands there and there is a logging road right over the tunnel. Now,

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: where is that tunnel from here?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: It's just about straight south of here.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How far?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: About three, four miles. But, of course, there is no road across there, just wild country. Hell, the river is right down below us. Hell, I've caught lots of fish in there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Big ones?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh, I've caught some pretty good. Hell, I've caught salmon in there. 14, 15 pounders. There was one spring, I caught 11 salmon down there. And the smallest one was three pound. From that to 15. Henry Benson told me he used to go fishing with you down there… henry, yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Is Henry still alive?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: He sure is… he lives in Onaway. He's pretty fat isn't he?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: No, no, I wouldn't say he's fat. He's pretty old. He's in his 80s. Yes, he's born right up here. He told me he used to pal around with you. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah, we're hundreds quite a little together, too. I think the last time I and Henry hunted together, he jumped out a big buck. That hog dressed 256 pounds. And I sent Henry home with half of that deer. He was breaking, well, his brother was breaking on the railroad up here. George is dead. George Benson and Nina, his older sister, I think she lives in Palouse. That's right. I saw her, too. She was there with his house when I stopped by.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Arthur, didn't you haul logs for the Bovill Hotel when they were building it?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yes, I hauled the logs up to the Benson's sawmill, up to the Dahlberg's sawmill, and then from the sorted lumber, we hauled the lumber to Bovill. And by God, mud came to the hubs and the wagons.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did Bovill look like then?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh, he was a pretty... No, I mean the town, the place where the, the site of the town. Hell, there was only one house up there, the old Warren Hub. And that old Warren cabin still stands there and that's over a hundred years old. There were three brothers of them, Warrens, Lewis Frank and Ellis. Oh, I can't think of the third one's name. I knew all of them. They were the first ones in that country. Yeah. They're homesteading and up there. Then, when Warrens come, he bought them out and he come from Texas. And he was a cowboy. And they shipped the cattle in from Texas to stop the ranshipping.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Is this Bovill? Who are you talking about? Bovill or Warren?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Bovill. Oh, yeah. Huh. He married a widow. She was the one that had the money. And then, when they get up here, they had twin girls. And I think one of them, the lady down here on the coast, some of them, maybe both of them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What kind of a guy was Bovill? What was he like? Was he an aristocrat?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh, he was a pretty good sized man, dark, complacent, kind of long mustache. There's a lot of it. Many are general Bovills. When we hauled lumber up there, it was always the hired men that unload the lumber and we'd go to dinner.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was the hotel like? What was it like inside? Was it nice?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh, to begin with, it was just a little log cabin. Then, they built a hotel up there and that got pretty good, a butcher shop. And hauled many beef up there and sold to the fellow veterans, the butcher shop.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: He built the hotel out of the lumber that you brought up there?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: You bet we hauled the lumber for that hotel. If I could see, and one thing I'd like to see them girls again now. One of them was up at Bovill here four or five years ago and visited. I think she had a car wreck and had a leg hurt pretty badly. So, I guess she's kind of a cripple. I think you're right. I think you're right. I know damn well I am.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, what was the place like before the lumber company came in?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh, it was timber all around it. And by God, it was a good fishing stream too. Hell, it was nothing to catch trout that long. And the same way all the way up the river here. Shoot the biggest catch on the creek down here. 186 trout in one day.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did you think of Bovill? What did I think of it?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: By God, old Bovill was a damn nice man. And by God, when you brought a load of lumber up there, by God, you got the cash right now. You didn't have to wait for it. He paid for the whole of them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Arthur, did you hear about the Agnes Leener killing? Did you hear about Agnes Leener getting killed?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yes, I do. And by God, I can put my fingers on her grave too.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What happened there?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh, that damn just gentleman, I have an idea, got her into the tunnel and raped her. And I suppose she put up a fight and then he just took and killed her. She's buried on the same lot that my neighbor, my notion is buried on down here on the Lutheran Cemetery. Yes, I knew Agnes Leener swung her quite a few times on the third floor.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was she a pretty girl?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yes, she was a nice girl. I wonder why he bothered her.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Had he known her for a long time?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, that damn damn outfit was just kind of an outlaw outfit anyway.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, after he killed her, did he shoot himself too or what happened?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: No, he shot himself and it wasn't his gun either. It was her brother's gun he used. And there was only one shell left in the gun. So he killed himself and he didn't make it so he didn't die before the next day.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did they do? Did they drag him out of there?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yeah, they took him out and I guess they took him into Volvo to the hospital and he died there. And he is buried on that poor man's graveyard in Moscow, right back to the main graveyard.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: He used five bullets before he got to himself?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: No, there was only a couple of three bullets in the gun, see. And he didn't have any more. I wonder if he thought he was going to get away with it. Well, see, he shot her and money shot one shot at her brother but he missed him. Money used to last one on himself and the gun went empty. Somebody told me that when people got him they dragged him out of there. They just didn't care whether they killed him or not anymore… well, they didn't… no man's gentleman says, oh, he got away with everything. He'll get out of that too but he didn't. I knew his dad well. He was road boss here for a good many years. I worked good many days for his dad. I hope he was a better guy than the son was. Oh, yeah. He was a good man.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did he, did old man Dillman have a bear that he took around the country?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh, yeah, he used to trap bear all over. And then he'd get out and sell bear meat and if he could trade bear meat to some of the people around the country and get a dozen eggs, he'd one of the soft boil that eggs, then he'd sit down and eat a dozen of eggs to the meat. And he leapt right on by. And I think I knew the girl too. Because we used to have a place right next to our school house and put near all the school moms that'd leave, that'd ride horse back, come into school in the morning and they'd leave the horse in our barn. Oh, you know this, hello, Commissioner over at Moscow? Ingle. Ingle. I think Ingle, Jerry Ingle. Yeah, hell, I knew his mother well before she was married. Yes, I've swung her in the walls a time or two too.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, what did you hear about this teacher getting killed?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, that's hard to say. You know there was, well, on that grade down there, shoot, there was several girls that was killed down there. And there was one from California that disappeared that they never did find. Hell, them girls got killed in a throat cut. And they claimed it was some of the university students from Pullman that done it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: That's over on the Big Bear grade going down towards Kendrick?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: No, it's on that other grade down there going down to the Clearwater. Hell, I've been down that grade two, three times.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Where does the road go from to get to the Clearwater?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: It's on the other side of Pullman. Oh. Instead of coming to Moscow, we go the other way down there. Yeah. Yes, I've been over that grade a couple, three times too.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh, there was one story I heard that you, there's one story, didn't Sam Samowich shoot a guy?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yes. And the other fella tried to kill him with an axe. And he caught Sam's shoulder, so it just hung. And Sam had his gun loaded out and T .B. Jones had it and T .B. Jones got the gun back. And Sam got the gun out and he says, I'll shoot him once and the steelkeeper come in. I'll shoot him twice and the steelkeeper come in. I'll shoot him three times, but then he goes down like a sober man. Hell, I knew Sam Samowich just about as well as I knew my brother. The camp was right over there and he was over there and after he got so he could get around, he'd sit around in the evening and patch watches with a bow and when they'd stop, he held Sam Samowich with a damn knife.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well how did that fight start?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, Sam was a...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Foreman?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Section foreman and he fired this fella, well this fella says, He can't, you can't either and he was going to kill him with an axe. That's how it started and that started right in the country road. The railroad crossed the country road down here at Moscow.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did Sam have the gun on him right at the time?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: No, T .P. Jones had just brought the gun back and handed it to him. Well did T .P.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: hand him the gun after he got axed or before?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Before he killed him. Well you know T .P. brought back the gun that morning after he went back to work. Because it was quite a lot of bow hunt trouble at that time and put near all the bosses carried the gun. And T .P. didn't have one so he borrowed Sam's so he could get one of his own. And when he got one of his own he got Sam's gun back.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did Sam kill this guy when he shot him?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh yeah, Sam killed him already. And I think that fella was buried right up there in the Bovill cemetery.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Why were they having trouble? Why were they carrying guns, the foremen?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well hell, there was always some of them coming around causing trouble in camp. And when they'd get one of them fellas coming around making trouble they'd run them out of the country. The camp was right over here, I've seen a lot of that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was that I .W .W.?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yeah, I .W .N. They called it I Won't Work. Another said I Won't Work. They all spelled I .W .N. see, it all spelled the same.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was it the I .W .W.'s that were causing the trouble?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Were they the reason they... No, they were causing trouble. One of them bastards come along you know and just sticks their head in the bunkhouse. They had trouble on boys and not damaging like every damn strike on boys and next morning there wouldn't be a man that would go to work. That's the way it went.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you ever hear that the I .W .W.'s were the ones that got better conditions in the camp?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well,… oh they got... I don't think they got any better food but they got maybe a little better pay… oh,

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: did the Potlatch Lumber Company, did they start the town at Deary or did somebody, did McGowan and Henry do it by themselves?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, McGowan, I think bought that land from Braylock and that stuff and then of course you got permission from the railroad company and the railroad company put in a depot. And they surveyed the town.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did McGowan work for Potlatch?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: No, they kind of worked for themselves. Oh yeah, they had offices right here in Potlatch, in Deary. Yes, I pointed out some of the government corners for them too. I knew putting the government corner in this country because I done a lot of hunting and every damn time I'd find a government corner I'd pay attention to it. And by God it was one thing, if I ever went to a government corner I could always go back. And I wouldn't need no compass neither. You take the timber and it's just as good as a compass. You look at a tree and by God you can tell who knows it himself.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, so you know all the big limbs is on the south side of the tree and the bark is darker on the north side, lighter on the north side of the tree than it is on the south side. And twelve o 'clock at any time the sun, as you can see, is a straight sun. There's a lot of people that don't know that. Hell, if I ever went to a place I could go back to it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would you ever get lost in these woods?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Not for very long. Unless it was a hell of a snowstorm that was twisting the trees around so you couldn't see. And snow would blow until you couldn't open your eyes. By now being turned around. But if you sit down, if you get turned down and just pull the coat off your head and sit down a while, by God pretty soon the world will turn right around and you'll come straight again. There's a lot of people that don't know that. By God, some people when they get good and lost, by God even if they get into your own house they don't know their own home.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Is that true?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: It's true… the damn rabbit's true because I seen it happen to my mother.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When I brought her in she says, what place is this?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: And she was riding home.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How had she gotten lost?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: I was picking up her birds and got turned around until I was a day off going.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: She just didn't know which way she was going at all?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: No, she didn't have no idea where she was going. Dad got lost one night cloudy night right in the woodshed and he couldn't find his way out of the woodshed. Lots of things have happened.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you find your mother when she was lost?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: You bet I did. I could track putting you as good as a dog and I had a dog that was a damn side better. I put him on the track and by God he found it. And I was right behind of him too.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How long had she been missing?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh yes, a couple of hours.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you give the dog some of her clothes to smell?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yes, I told the dog to go find him and by God he took right off. And by God I was right behind of him too. And those days I could travel putting her like a razor. I had no trouble but me to take a 35 mile blanket roll. After working all day and start from Tennessee and walk in here next morning at a 30 mile hike.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You just go all night?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yes… that must have been hard. It was and generally no surface road and the dust always shot horses. You would just dust that deep in the road. Every four or five miles you would have to stop and take your shoes off and shake the dirt out of your shoes to be able to walk.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You would go a foot all the way?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: You are damn right I would walk all the way. I know one time I started from down there in Tennessee about five o 'clock in the evening and I walked in here and the folks were sitting down to breakfast. When Potlatch came in here and started buying the timber I heard they bought the timber very very cheap. Well hell, all the timber they bought was the time and they bought that for a dollar a thousand. And then they just counted the trees and then trees had to be 16 inches or through or bigger at this jump. Well all the fur and time right they didn't sell that at all. And when they got the timber deed they got a deed for the timber in such a section. And fur and time right, white fur and sprues. And time right that was all they gave. They got that for nothing.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So which were the species that they wanted? What were the kinds of trees they counted in the survey? What kinds of trees did they count in the survey?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Just yellow pine and white pine. Black pine and all the rest of it wasn't counted at all. Then when they got, bought it, the state gave them the timber deed, the state gave them the rest of the timber. And of course the farmers that had homesteads used the same darn thing. The potlucks didn't have warehouses, what it was called then, didn't buy I don't think more than a tenth of the timber and pay for it. The rest of it was all they gave. So when you were out with Bill Helmer the only timber he cruised was the white pine and the yellow pine. That's all he counted. That's all they counted because there, well he was more to open up the lines and take out the railroad squares. The log, he wasn't a cruising much unless there was somebody that wanted to sell a piece of land then he'd cruise it for them.

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: And they'd walk it the same way and buy them the Milwaukee cruisers. They'd cruise it and by God you could sell your timber right at home and you'd get a check right at home and then you'd do the rest of it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was it a pretty good deal for the homesteaders or did they get rooked?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh, the homesteaders didn't get much out of it. It was the company that was getting all the drag out of it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: All the what?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: It was the company that was getting all the property.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you sell timber to them, your father? Or you sell timber?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yeah, my father sold the timber on the place here and then by God it was ten years that it stood here that we couldn't do a damn thing. Unless on best 40 he saved the black pine on that so you could cut out the black pine and make wood. What you're saying is that Potlatch didn't help the people so much as they helped themselves. They helped themselves a whole lot more than helped the people. Of course, it got so the people could get work all right and camp.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you remember what it was like snowshoeing with Bill Helmer or snowshoeing in the winter?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Damn right I remember what it was like and I walked a good many hundred miles on snowshoes. Tell me how that was done.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How did you do it?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, them snowshoes. Well, there was long ones. Them were the trampers. But the barefoot, they were just kind of three -cornered. You could walk and turn around them. That's what we always used in the woods. Hell, I had a set of snowshoes till the old buildings went up and they went up. Hell, I snowshoes a lot of them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, could you use the same trail over again? Could you use the same trail again?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Hell, yes… yes, use the same trail over and over. And then we had the skis. I used to ski a lot. Yet it was nothing for me to make fifty and sixty foot jumps on the steep hillside.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you see that mountain up there? Which direction?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: The ... Butte. Oh yeah. We'd ski from the top of that plane to the bottom on skis in the early days. In the early days, by gosh, I have a mess. No, got deep. We'd ski down here on the brakes and kettle a deer every once in a while. But now we run short of something to eat.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You mean you just camp out in the winter? You just camp out down there?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: No, we'd go down in the morning and come back at night.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And kill a deer for dinner?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Why, we'd kill a deer and then make a pike sack out of the deer and come back at night, come home at night. I've carried quite a few deer on my back.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Where was your lower place? The place where you wintered? On the ridge? You know where the steel schoolhouse used to be?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: I don't think so. Well, that steel schoolhouse was on our place.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Where? Now whereabouts would that be now? You know where Waha Lake is?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yeah. Well, it'd be north and east of Waha Lake.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You know where the Four Corners is down there? And you know where the churches down there?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: I think I do, I'm not sure.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: That's where? In there?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yeah… well, there was two churches down there. The Lutheran and then there was the American church. And it wasn't too low.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, you know where Ed Hall's at?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh yeah. The Lutheran church, I think, was right at the corner of the place where Ed Hall's at.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So you weren't too far from his place? You were pretty close to his place?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yeah, but further north. A couple of miles further north.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Are you thinking of Atwater Lake? Huh? Are you thinking of Atwater Lake?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yeah. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh, do you remember what instruments you used to survey with Bill Helmer?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yes, I compass.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you go to school? What grade did you go up to?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, to tell the truth, the way it is now, I don't think it'd be more than about the third grade now. Because, hell, if I go to school, the best was two and three months. Well, what you learnt one time, you forgot to the next one. So what little I know, I've studied that mission.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How old were you when you stopped going to school?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh, about fourteen, fifteen. Oh,… i was going to ask you a little more about the herding of cattle.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I was going to ask you, what was the grass like that the cattle grazed on? Huh? What was the grass like that the cattle grazed on?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh, it was just common pine grass. It's the same kind of grass as it is now. But those days, it wasn't worth it that damn grass would get that high… maybe two feet… by God, there was, and the Indians kept it burnt off, there was pressure down here between the big timber that you could take a mowing machine and a team of horses and mow grass in among the big timber and rake it up. Now, by God, you can't walk in among your big timber.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Are you sure the Indians burnt the grass here?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, either the Indians or the lightning. It was nothing those days to have several lightning storms during the summer.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: But you think the Indians did it?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, one day I was up here, one day leaving the fall, they weren't particularly about the fire. Hell, I know they used to camp up here. When they'd leave, hell, there'd always be a smoke behind them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you think they burnt the country to make better grazing for their horses?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yes… yes, easier hunting, getting around. And you know, the Indians, the bucks, they didn't do anything. They'd go out and hunt, but the damn squirrels, they'd be the ones that'd have to pack in the meat and take care of the hives and make demarcations and all that. And try the meat. That was the squirrels' work. The bucks wouldn't do that. And by God, from the white starting coming in here, there's a damn good many half -bridge and quarter -bridge right around here now. Even some of my neighbors had got quite a lot of Indian blood in them. Because when she'd move in with a white man, she didn't have to work so hard because he'd bring the meat in and dress that. She wouldn't have to do that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So it was easier for her to live with a white man, you say? So it was easier to live with a white?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yes. Hell, right. And mostly Frenchmen that marriage caused. I didn't know there were Frenchmen in here. Oh yeah, there was quite a few Frenchmen in here. There's several of the neighbor women right here that's got Indian blood in them and quite a little too. And one of my friends is married to a full -blooded squirrel. She's around 90 years old.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did those marriages work out pretty good usually with an Indian and white?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: My God, they got along good. They got along at times better than a lot of the whites did.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So marriages didn't always work out in the old days either, huh?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: There's often they don't work out now… oh hell… well, you know, in the late 19th century, her mother and father were always the fighters and whipping the kids. Oh, it would be kind of fun to, if I could hear and see, to see Nana again.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How come you never got married?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Too damn many people had too many things to say.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What do you mean?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Too damn many people had too damn many lies to tell. And there were a lot of things that they didn't know a damn thing about.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And you know how that is?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: A lot of people got to tell something about somebody that they don't know a damn thing about. And it would be a great big long lie. I'm not sure I know why, what that means. I don't know exactly what you're saying about why that means you didn't get married yourself.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: People trying to push you into it, is that it?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: No, they just told the girls that I went with too damn many lies. I don't think I would have had very much trouble to have gotten hang of ancient years stage right here and there. Well there's lots of guys, lots of old timers that are bachelors. Oh, there was quite a few.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh, what were you going to say? Huh? Were you going to say something?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: No.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When you say that the whites ruined the country, the Indians took good care of it, what do you mean… how's that?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: You told me that the whites ruined the country and the Indians took good care of it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What do you mean?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well the whites come in here and they ruined all the timber and all the berries and all the fish and if that ain't ruined it, I'd like to know what was. And you know as far as that goes, this country, all the United States, isn't a country at all. Just all kinds of nations moved in, all kinds of people. It isn't one nation at all. It's just a mixed up bunch. And you know that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you think, ever think about leaving this area and going someplace else?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: No,… because there's been too damn many that want to get me out of here and they're still bothering the heads about me staying here. Well I was thinking about when you were a young man. Oh, when you were 20 or 30. Well, Mother was alive and I agreed with Dad that I'd see Mother through and I did. I didn't do like the other folks, go and marry a young girl and bring her in to live with your mother. That's entirely wrong. But there was lots of them that were young men and they always got a little trouble in the family too.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Why, because the girl and the mother don't get along?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: They get out of the time to do it. Well the mother, they're living on what the mother swarms, say. Well she thinks she's got more right than the young woman. Well they kind of get an argument over it. And you know, it isn't fair. It isn't fair to bring a young woman in to live as an old mother -in -law. I wouldn't think about it. And that's why I stayed single too.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What year did your mother die?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Dad died 1911. 1911. No, I was just a farmer's brand.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you have a brand on them?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: No. Hooker's cattle was A8 and Iverberg's was B. And I heard of the cattle for three years and I lost only one head. And I fell into a prospect hole so I could go for battle.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did some people have trouble with rustlers in those days?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh, I guess there was some cattle butchers alright but I didn't have any trouble. Because a lot of them, you know, wouldn't have herders with them but I was right with the cattle all the time. And all knew I had a damn good dog that could drive. And you probably, they probably knew you had a good gun too. Yeah, and a good many of them knew I could use it. I was good enough to stand up 60, 70 feet and shoot flies when they'd land on the picket fence. That's awful good Arthur. That's awful good.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How old did, what, what were you going to say? How old did the cattle get before you would ship them to market?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well they'd take them down on the place they had home places and keep them there. And then they'd sell them at home there. And Hooker, Weeden, they're shifting a bunch from Montana and there were two cattle loads in that bunch. I got the promise to kill them. So I shot them down on the ridge.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Butchered them too?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Uh huh.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Butchered them too? Did you butcher them?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yeah… when they were going to butcher them, they had me go out and shoot them. I had a damn good horse. I could ride pretty close to them. I'd ride that horse back and then I'd slide off on the horse and then my gun over the saddle and kill the cattle out in the field.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How close would you get to them?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh, 100, 150 feet. That was nothing for me.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Where did you aim for?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Generally right side of the head of the forehead.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Which ever comes the hand in?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh hell, I wouldn't shoot through the body. That would have driven too much meat. In those days you had to be kind of careful too. In goes the young man. They were going to butcher a wild one they had. By God, I guess they shot about 30 times just that damn thing and couldn't get it. Finally I killed it for him. I was a pretty good shot on the run. It didn't make much difference whether I did or stood on the run. I could generally stop it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would they cut the throat right away? They?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: They would have landed. They were a couple of miles behind and that poor damn beef was ablating all over.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh, you said that Green saved the bank in Troy during the Depression? Huh? Did you say that Frank Green saved the bank in Troy? How did that happen?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well he happened to have enough money on hand and all in other banks so he could take over. So he really took over the bank in Troy. And it wouldn't have surprised me. I think that's how Green's money is at the back in that bank right now.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was that Depression anywhere near as bad as the one in 1893?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Yeah. And later you know there was being a couple of Depression. There was one in 1982. It's really true that the men didn't have enough..… wait.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How much money did it take to file on a homestead back then? Just a few dollars?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: I think it was six dollars and about ten to prove that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And people couldn't afford that much money?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Hell, there wasn't that much money, hardly that much money in the county.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What in hell would you do if you had to go out and work for a living and only get fifty and seventy -five cents a day?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: A man worked fifteen and sixteen hours a day to get that fifty cents. I've worked many a day for less than a dollar a day. And worked damn hard too. I just don't see how people could get by on that little money. Well, if they hadn't had a cow or two and a few chickens, they wouldn't. That was generally their life form. Eggs and bread. And maybe after they got a cow, a little milk to drink. And then they'd cook marsh. Milk and water together and a little salt and use flour in it and cook it and make a stiff marsh out of it. That was generally their supper. No, I wish some of the smart eggs that have come in here now, trying to show the whole time without walking on the trails, had to put in a winger in order for some same condition. And maybe they wouldn't be so goddamn flat.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Harper, do you think this country changed a lot when Potlatch came in?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh, they all changed so it got a little work for the people. They could get out and work and get a little work and it got so that they could cut a little wood and ship out because the Nazi country didn't have any timber in all. Moscow and that way, they'd buy wood.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Has it changed more now than it did when Potlatch came in? Is this more of a change than that was?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh yeah… well, it wasn't so much of a starvation because all those fellows that were able to work could get out and work in the camp. Like I hear, when the camp was over here, how I sawed logs and the snow was deep. And the boss over there said, oh hell, you can't saw logs alone. I said, by God, I can try. And after a few days he found out that I made more money than the two men in camp. Because they'd have to shuffle that deep snow while I'd get right up on the logs and saw down and saw the logs. They'd have to have seen the logs and never paid much attention to it. Just let them go in through one ear and out through the other one. And mostly all of them were Swedish stories because there was more Swedes than anything else in this country.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you remember the kind of stories they used to tell? These lies?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Oh, I can't say that I paid too much attention to them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you have any ways of predicting the weather? Any signs that you use?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: No… nothing else. When the stars fall and one thing another, then you could put near a jet and then some dogs. You could put near a tower and there was a change in the weather all right.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What's a sundog?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, there'd be a long streak on the side of the sun. You could see that every once in a while when it was bad weather. And you could tell pretty well when the geese and the ducks would go over to whether it was going to be a hard or light winter. If they'd come early in the fall and go south, they would bet on the hard winter. But if they'd wait late, they'd have a light winter.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about spring? Did you have any way of knowing when spring was going to come?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well,… you know, a fella kind of looked quite a little, and there was a dark or the light of the moon too. He went by the moon quite a little. And the same way with plant and grain. Plant grain in the light of the moon while the sign is way up in the body. And if you want to cut a hog or a pig's weight, the sign gets down towards the bottom of the foot and the wooden blade. And like wheat and oats, plant that in the light of the moon. And spuds, plant them in the dark of the moon. Spuds and motorbikes and turnips and carrots and stuff like that, plant them in the dark of the moon.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Why is that?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, it seems like the signs and the weather has got a whole lot to do with. There is a lot of people that don't believe in the signs, but those two brothers down here are thrust for them for years. And by God knew couldn't change them and they always had the best grain of any of the people in the country. So it had something to do with it and by God they knew it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did your father plant by signs too?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: No, brothers didn't grow much by signs. These fellas did everything by signs. These two brothers. These two brothers though, they did everything by signs. Oh yeah, some of them do. Now like Tom Fireboy up there, he says, oh no, he says, the moon ain't got nothing to do with it. By George the moon and the sun has got the whole thing to do with the weather. And by God, you know, even raising cattle, it makes a hell of a difference what time of the day you raise cattle. You breed that cow too. Whether you want a bull calf or a heifer calf. People don't believe that, but by God that's truth because I've tried that terrible time.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Which time of the day do you use?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Morning for a heifer and evening for a bull calf.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Are there harvest signs too? Are there signs for harvesting too?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Now here the mckinnis,… all of them just wanted a girl in the family. And by God, every child that's been born is being a boy. By God, I think it's the yesterday time they've got the moon in them. Whether it was in the morning or in the evening.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Have you ever heard about any ghosts? Have you ever heard about ghosts?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: No… i thought maybe there might be signs for death too. Well, it could be, but I don't know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What do you think?

segments.speaker: Arthur Bjerke
segments.words: Well, in all late years I paid any attention to anything. So I forgot about everything I paid attention to when I was young. Well, it seems to me that you still remember a lot. I was able to do any good for the kids. I'm glad for that because the kids have always been my friends. Now Ronnie Halstead, he's got a little girl and a boy. They usually come down and visit with me about every other day. And boy, that little boy has a real talking machine. And I pretty always managed to have a piece of candy or something for him.
